answer: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is the field of building computer systems that do tasks which normally need human thinking [01-001]. Those tasks include recognising pictures, understanding spoken or written language, and making predictions from past information [01-001].

Machine learning is one way of building AI [02-001]. It is the approach that depends on learning from data [02-003]. Instead of a programmer writing every rule by hand, the system learns patterns from examples and adjusts itself until it can make useful predictions about new examples it has not seen before [02-001].
Overfitting is when a system performs well on training data but poorly on test data because it has memorised the examples rather than learning a general pattern [03-002].

Narrow AI is built to do one specific task or a small set of related tasks well, performing its task within limits without being able to simply switch to a different task on its own [04-001]. In contrast, general AI (sometimes called artificial general intelligence) would be a system able to learn and perform a wide range of intellectual tasks the way a person can, allowing it to move between subjects, transfer what it learned in one area to another, and handle problems it was never specifically built for [04-002].

A spam filter is given thousands of emails, each labelled as spam or not spam [02-002]. The system finds patterns in these labelled examples, such as certain words, links, or sender habits, and uses them to judge new emails [02-002].
The quality of training examples matters because if the examples are few, unbalanced, or wrong, the system learns the wrong patterns [02-004].
A system trained on sunny photos might fail on night photos because it learns the patterns it sees rather than the patterns intended by the people building it [03-003].

An AI system can be fair in some cases and unfair in others, depending on how it was built and tested [06-002]. AI systems learn from data created by people, and if the data contains gaps or bias, the system can repeat those problems in its answers [06-002].

An AI answer can sound confident and still be wrong because fluency is not the same as accuracy [07-001]. A system can give a confident answer that is incorrect, incomplete, or made up, which is sometimes called hallucination, and this can happen even when the answer looks well organised [07-001]. Additionally, a tool built from narrow or biased data will tend to give narrow or biased answers, even when its wording sounds confident [03-004].
